original_question: For distinct digits a1, ..., an chosen from {0,1,2,...,9} with 1 < n < 9, determine how many distinct prime numbers can be formed using all of those digits, and more generally ask the same question when a1, ..., an are distinct positive integers. Also, for a fixed digit a, determine how many occurrences of a appear in the decimal expansion of the nth prime, of n!, and of n^n, and ask the analogous question for a general nonnegative integer a.
target_in_paper: Unsolved Problem 3(a)-(b) in the paper’s unnumbered opening catalogue of problems. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft already tracks the paper very closely: it captures both subparts of Unsolved Problem 3, namely (a) the count of distinct primes obtainable from a prescribed set of distinct decimal digits with 1 < n < 9, together with the stated extension to distinct positive integers, and (b) the count of occurrences of a fixed digit in the decimal expansion of the n-th prime, of n!, and of n^n, together with the analogous extension from digits to a general nonnegative integer. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))
missing_details: Part (a) should explicitly say that the setting is base 10 and that “using all those digits” means forming integers whose decimal representation uses each of a1, ..., an exactly once. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))

For the extension from digits to distinct positive integers, a stand-alone formulation should specify how the integers are used to build a number; the natural paper-faithful reading is by concatenating their decimal expansions in some order, but the paper itself leaves that construction implicit. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))

Because 0 is allowed among the digits in part (a), a self-contained statement should exclude permutations beginning with 0; the paper does not state this convention explicitly. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))

Part (b) should define the counting operation explicitly, e.g. as the number of occurrences of the digit a in the decimal expansion of a given integer, and it should identify the n-th prime as p_n if that notation is introduced. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))

For the extension “more generally: when a ∈ N,” a stand-alone version should explain that one is then counting occurrences of the decimal block representing a, not a single digit; the paper does not specify an overlap convention for multi-digit blocks. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))

The nearby comment shows that the question is about exact counts rather than merely asymptotic approximations, since the sizes of p_n, n!, and n^n change irregularly as n increases. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))
refined_question: In base 10, (a) for a fixed integer n with 1 < n < 9 and distinct digits a1, ..., an ∈ {0,1,2,...,9}, determine how many distinct prime numbers are obtained by permuting these digits so that each is used exactly once, excluding permutations with leading digit 0; more generally, for n ∈ N* and distinct positive integers a1, ..., an, determine how many distinct primes are obtained by concatenating the decimal expansions of a1, ..., an in all possible orders; and (b) for a fixed digit a ∈ {0,1,2,...,9}, determine the number of occurrences of a in the decimal expansion of the n-th prime p_n, of n!, and of n^n, and more generally ask the analogous question for the decimal block corresponding to a fixed nonnegative integer a. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))
justification: The draft is essentially a near-verbatim paraphrase of Unsolved Problem 3(a)-(b): the hypotheses 1 < n < 9, the set {0,1,...,9}, the extension to distinct positive integers, and the three sequences “the n-th prime,” n!, and n^n all match the paper’s statement. I therefore kept the target narrow and did not shift to neighboring digit-pattern questions such as Unsolved Problem 10 (prescribed digit strings inside primes, n!, or n^n) or Unsolved Problem 17(a) (primes among expressions ap_n + b, n!, or n^n). The only sharpening needed was to make explicit the decimal/base-10 setting, the once-each use of the listed digits, the concatenation reading in the positive-integer generalization, and the occurrence-count interpretation in part (b); the comment immediately following Problem 3 also explains why simple analytic formulas are delicate, because the sizes of p_n, n!, and n^n jump from n to n+1. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))
